--- title: "Functions" subtitle: "Applying R to Lifestyle and Brain Health Research" author: "Ashlyn Barry" institute: "University of Wisconsin - Madison" date: 2026-09-09 image: "../../../images/thumbnails/functions.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, "../../../styles/styleReveal.scss"] slide-number: true preview-links: auto logo: https://brand.ku.edu/sites/brand/files/styles/wide_col_xl_6/public/images/2020/KUMarksLogo.png footer: "R for Lifestyle and Brain Health (R-LAB)" transition: slide background-transition: fade highlight-style: github code-line-numbers: true code-block-bg: true incremental: false date-format: long embed-resources: true execute: echo: true eval: false freeze: auto --- ## What are functions? ::: {.highlight-box} A function is a machine that takes something in, does a job to it, and gives something back out. For example, think about a blender: ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ![](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcSSZgQQ8QIhNMSEORXy1jcBFKcOgTDmWJLGc42Q9HFdPw&s=10) ::: ::: {.column} - Input → "ingredients" you put into the function: *fruit* - Function → machine's task: *blend* - Output → resulting product: *smoothie* ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} blender <- function(fruit) { smoothie <- blend(fruit) return(smoothie) } ``` ::: ## Functions have three main parts A function is a machine (blender): input (fruit) goes in, the machine (blender) completes a task, and output (smoothie) comes out. But what actually happens inside the machine? ::: {.highlight-box} Every function is built from three parts: *arguments*, *body*, and *environment* ::: - **Arguments** (`formals()`) → input, or ingredients you feed in (e.g., fruit) - **Body** (`body()`) → how the function works, or actual steps of how fruit gets blended - **Environment** (`environment()`) → everything else the function can access, or the 'kitchen' the blender sits in ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Environment example: adding milk to the smoothie milk <- "Half cup of milk" # milk accessible to blender in environment (i.e., R knows what you mean by milk) blender <- function(fruit) { # fruit assigned as an argument smoothie <- blend(fruit, milk) # milk is not an argument, but available in environment return(smoothie) # smoothie made from fruit and milk } ``` ::: Milk was never passed in as an argument, but the blender can 'grab' the milk because it is in the 'blender's kitchen', or the 'function's environment'. ::: {.tip-box} The function (blender) is assigned its environment (kitchen) automatically when it is built and never forgets it. R calls this *lexical scoping* (more on this later). ::: ## Attributes Functions also have extra 'labels' of information called *attributes* `attr()`. In our example, think of sticky notes attached to the blender. One particularly useful attribute is `srcref` (*source reference*), which is like a sticky note with the smoothie recipe. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} blender <- function(fruit) { # Blend the fruit into a smoothie smoothie <- blend(fruit) return(smoothie) } attr(blender, "srcref") #> function(fruit) { #> # Blend the fruit into a smoothie #> smoothie <- blend(fruit) #> return(smoothie) #> } ``` ::: ## Primitive functions ::: {.highlight-box} We just learned that every function is built from three parts: *arguments*, *body*, and *environment*. **Primitive functions break this rule (sigh!)** ::: - Small set of functions that skip the traditional three-part structure - Instead of running R code, they connect to **C code**: language R itself is built on - Since primitive functions are not "built" the normal way, arguments, body, and environments are all `NULL` ::: {.tip-box} Think of these as functions with no visible "recipe" at all; they are wired straight into R's engine rather than written out explicitly. :::
Primitive functions come in two types: **builtin** or **special** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sum #> function (..., na.rm = FALSE) .Primitive("sum") typeof(sum) #> [1] "builtin" `[` #> .Primitive("[") typeof(`[`) #> [1] "special" ``` ::: ## First-class functions: They are just objects! ::: {.highlight-box} So far we've treated functions like special machines. But in R, a function is just another type of **object**. ::: ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - There's no special syntax needed to "declare" a function - You create it with `function()`, then give it a name with `<-` — just like assigning a number to a name ::: ::: {.column} ![](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/diagrams/functions/first-class.png){.nostretch} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f01 <- function(x) { sin(1 / x^2) } ``` ::: Because functions are just objects, they don't *need* a name at all. **Anonymous functions** run the same way but are never assigned a name. This is useful if you only plan on running the analysis once, defeating the purpose of assigning it a long-term name. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} unlist(lapply(mtcars, function(x) length(unique(x)))) #> mpg cyl disp hp drat wt qsec vs am gear carb #> 25 3 27 22 22 29 30 2 2 3 6 ``` ::: Functions can also be stored inside other objects, like a *list*. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} funs <- list( half = function(x) x / 2, double = function(x) x * 2 ) ``` ::: ## Invoking a function A function is usually called by placing the arguments inside parentheses next to the function name. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(1:10, na.rm = TRUE) #> [1] 5.5 ``` ::: In some instances, the arguments are contained within an existing list or data structure. You can use `do.call` to get the arguments from a list instead of typing them all out by hand. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} args <- list(1:10, na.rm = TRUE) do.call(mean, args) # do.call(function, arguments list) #> [1] 5.5 ``` ::: ## Function composition ::: {.highlight-box} Most analyses you conduct will likely involve more than one function. **Composition** refers to chaining functions together so the output of one becomes the input of the next. ::: Base R gives you two main ways to achieve this: *Option 1: Save each step as its own variable (Intermediate Results)* - Pros: easy to read and write, especially if sharing code with others - Cons: can create a lot of unnecessary intermediate objects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} square <- function(x) x^2 deviation <- function(x) x - mean(x) x <- 1:20 # Saving intermediate results out <- deviation(x) out <- square(out) out <- mean(out) out <- sqrt(out) ``` ::: *Option 2: Nest the functions inside each other (Nested)* - Pros: no extra variables - Cons: 'inside out' reading, which can be difficult to follow ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Nested sqrt(mean(square(deviation(x)))) ``` ::: ::: {.tip-box} Both versions calculate the exact same thing; they're just two different ways of writing the same sequence of steps. ::: *Option 3:* `magrittr` The `magrittr` package uses binary operator called the pipe `%>%`, which read as "and then". The basic idea is to take what is on the left and then feed it into the function on the right. - Pros: read code in straightforward fashion without intermediate objects - Cons: requires additional package and slightly more advanced understanding of R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(magrittr) x %>% deviation() %>% square() %>% mean() %>% { paste0("Square root of ", ., " is ", round(sqrt(.), 2)) } ``` ::: ## Lexical scoping {.title-slide} ::: {.highlight-box} A function's environment (its "kitchen") is fixed the moment the function is built, not when it's used. **Lexical scoping** is the rule that R looks up values based on *where the function was written*, not *where it's called from*. ::: Lexical scoping follows four rules: 1) Name masking 2) Functions vs Variables 3) Fresh start 4) Dynamic lookup ## Rule 1: Name masking If a name exists both *inside* and *outside* a function, R uses the inside version. The inside version *masks* or hides the outside version. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 10 f <- function() { x <- 1 x } f()() #> [1] 1 ``` ::: If a name isn't defined inside a function, R looks one level up to find it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- 2 f <- function() { y } f() #> [1] 2 ``` ::: *Step outward until you find it*: R keeps looking further out, all the way to the global environment, until it finds a match. ::: {.tip-box} Applied to the kitchen analogy: if an ingredient isn't right next to the blender, R will check the counter, then the pantry, then the kitchen, then the house... ::: ## Rule 2: Functions vs Variables If a name is being used as a variable, R looks for a variable. If a name is being used as a function (i.e., followed by parentheses), R looks for a function, even if a variable with that name is closer (per Rule 1). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- function(x) x + 1 f <- function() { n <- 5 n(10) } f() #> [1] 11 ``` ::: - Outside f(), 'n' is a function that adds 1 to whatever you give it - Inside f(), a second 'n' is created, where it is set equal to 5 - The last line, n(10) uses parentheses, telling R you want the function version of n - R sees n(...) and knows it needs a function, so it skips over the variable n <-- 5 and keeps looking outward until it finds a function version of n - f() thus is 10 + 1 = 11 :::{.highlight-box} The number 5 and function x + 1 are both named 'n', and they coexist without conflict because R checks *how* the name is being used (as a value or as a function). ::: ## Rule 3: Fresh start Every time a function is called, R builds it a new, empty environment. Nothing from the previous call is remembered. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} add_one <- function() { x <- 0 x <- x + 1 x } add_one() #> [1] 1 add_one() #> [1] 1 ``` ::: - Each time add_one() runs, it starts fresh: x is set to 0, then 1 is added - The second call does not remember the first: instead of adding one to the previous answer, it starts fresh with 0 + 1 - In other words, x from the first call is thrown away the moment the function finishes, so the second call builds x from scratch ## Rule 4: Dynamic lookup Lexical scoping tells R *where* to look for a value, but R doesn't check where that value is *until* the function is run (not when it's created). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function() x + 1 x <- 15 f() #> [1] 16 x <- 20 f() #> [1] 21 ``` ::: - F() doesn't have its own 'x', so it looks one level out to find it (Rule 1) - Which value of 'x' depends on whatever 'x' is *at the moment f() runs*, not what 'x' was when f() was first written ## Lazy Evaluation {.title-slide} Function arguments are **lazy**: they are not evaluated until they are actually used inside the function. If an argument is not used, it will not be evaluated. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(x) { 10 } # No error is generated because x is never used. f(stop("This is an error!")) #> [1] 10 ``` ::: - f() never uses 'x' in its body; it returns "10" no matter what is passed in - 'stop("This is an error!")' would normally halt everything, but it is never triggered because R is not told to evaluate x in the body of its function ## Why laziness matters **1) A value is calculated once, no matter how many times it is used** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} double <- function(x) { message("Calculating...") x * 2 } f <- function(x) { c(x, x) } f(double(20)) #> Calculating... #> [1] 40 40 ``` ::: "Calculating..." only prints once, even though x appears twice inside f(). R evaluates it the first time it's needed, then reuses that same result. **2) Default argument values can refer to other arguments** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(x = 1, y = x + 1) { c(x, y) } f() #> [1] 1 2 ``` ::: - y's default is an expression of 'x + 1', not a fixed number - Since arguments are *lazy*, 'y' isn't evaluated until it is needed. By the time y is needed, x is already assigned 1, so 'y' becomes 2 ## The ... (dot-dot-dot) ::: {.highlight-box} `...` (pronounced dot-dot-dot) let's a function accept any number of arguments without naming them ahead of time, which can be used directly or passed along to another function. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(...) { sum(...) } f(1, 2, 3) #> [1] 6 ``` ::: - `...` uses argments given in f(): 1, 2, and 3 - Those arguments are passed to `sum()` ## Errors with ... Because `...` accepts *anything*, a misspelled argument name won't cause an error; it will just get ignored and disappear. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(x, ...) { mean(x, ...) } f(c(1, 2, NA), na.rm = TRUE) #> [1] 1.5 f(c(1, 2, NA), na_rm = TRUE) #> [1] NA ``` ::: - The second call misspells `na.rm` as `na_rm` - R doesn't catch the error; it treats `na_rm` as an used argument in `...` ::: {.tip-box} `...` is helpful for writing flexible, reusable functions, but typos in arguments get ignored instead of flagged. ::: ## Exiting a function A function exits in one of two ways: by *returning a value* or by *throwing an error*. A return can be implicit (R returns the last line) or explicit (you use `return()` yourself). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Implicit - the last evaluated expression is returned automatically f <- function(x) { if (x < 10) { 0 } else { 10 } } f(9) #> [1] 0 # Explicit - return() exits the function immediately with that value f <- function(x) { if (x < 10) { return(0) } return(10) } f(9) #> [1] 0 ``` ::: Both versions do the same thing: `return()` is optional but makes it *explicit* to what is being sent back and when. ## Errors Errors occur when a function cannot complete its assigned task. It uses `stop()` to stop the execution of the function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} double <- function(x) { if (!is.numeric(x)) { stop("x must be numeric") } x * 2 } double(10) #> [1] 20 double("cats") #> Error in double("cats") : x must be numeric ``` ::: ::: {.tip-box} A clear `stop()` halts the function and displays an error message telling user exactly what went wrong, instead of the function failing confusingly down the line. ::: ## Function forms {.title-slide} Functions can be written in four different styles, depending on where the function name sits relative to arguments. - **Prefix**: name comes *before* arguments, `print(x)` - **Infix**: name comes *between* its arguments, `x + y` - **Replacement**: modifies values by *assignment*, `names(x) <- c("a", "b")` - **Special**: *built in* language features like `if`, `for`, and `[[` ## Prefix Functions Most common functions in R and what you have been seeing throughout this presentation. Function name comes first, followed by its arguments in parentheses. R lets you supply those arguments in a few different ways. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} f <- function(age, weight) { list(age = age, weight = weight) } # By position f(30, 70) #> $age #> [1] 30 #> #> $weight #> [1] 70 # By name — order no longer matters f(weight = 70, age = 30) #> $age #> [1] 30 #> #> $weight #> [1] 70 ``` ::: ::: {.tip-box} Arguments can be matched by their *position* (order listed) or *name*, which overrides their position. ::: ## Infix functions Infix functions take two arguments with the function name *between* them, like `+` or `-`. This is calling the style you use everytime you write `x + y`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 5 y <- 2 x + y #> [1] 7 `+`(x, y) #> [1] 7 ``` ::: :::{.tip-box} Infix functions are regular functions that you can call in a natural, readable way. ::: ## Replacement Functions Replacement functions look like they're modifying a value *in place*, but they're just regular functions with a special name ending in `<-`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} `first<-` <- function(x, value) { x[1] <- value x } x <- c(1, 2, 3) first(x) <- 100 x #> [1] 100 2 3 ``` ::: ## Special forms There are many language features in R that are written in special ways but also have prefix forms. | Special | Prefix | |:---------:|:---------:| | (x) | \`(\`(x) | | {x} | \`{\`(x) | | x[i] | \`[\`(x, i) | | x[[i]] | \`[[\`(x, i) | | if (cond) true | \`if\`(cond, true) | | if (cond) true else false | \`if\`(cond, true, false) | | for(var in seq) action | \`for\`(var, seq, action) | | while(cond) action | \`while\`(cond, action) | | repeat expr | \`repeat\`(expr) | | next | \`next\`() | | break | \`break\`() | | function(arg1, arg2) {body} | \`function\`(alist(arg1, arg2), body, env) ## Practice creating your own functions! ::: {.highlight-box} Time to build a few functions! First try them on your own, and then we will walk through the solutions together. ::: **1) Write a basic function** Write a function called `square()` that takes one number and returns its square (e.g., `square(4)` should return '16') **2) Write a function with a default argument** Write a function called `greet()` that takes a name and returns a greeting with "Hello, [name]!". Give `name` a default value of "friend", so `greet()` with no input returns "Hello, friend!". **3) Write a function using `...`** Write a function called `add_all()` that takes any number of numeric arguments and returns their sum (e.g., `add_all(1, 2, 3)` should return '6') :::{.tip-box} **Hint:** think back to how `sum()` was used inside the `...` example! ::: ## Solutions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. Write a basic function square <- function(x) { x^2 } square(4) #> [1] 16 # 2. Write a function with a default argument greet <- function(name = "friend") { paste0("Hello, ", name, "!") } greet() #> [1] "Hello, friend!" greet("Ashlyn") #> [1] "Hello, Ashlyn!" # 3. Write a function using '...' add_all <- function(...) { sum(...) } add_all(1, 2, 3) #> [1] 6 ``` :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
